stories.title_en: Swapping Whole Fake Ingots for Real Silver

paragraphs.en: A merchant from Quanzhou Prefecture named Sun Tao was an honest man with the bearing of an elder. Carrying over a hundred taels of silver, he traveled to Nanjing to buy cloth. At Yanshan, he boarded a boat and chanced upon a swindler named Wang Lan. Wang falsely claimed to be from Xinghua Prefecture; since their dialects were similar, they shared the boat for several days and got along well. Wang soon realized Sun was a simple, honest man who could easily be fooled. Making some excuse, Wang said he would go ashore at Wuhu to buy goods. On board, he mentioned he hadn't yet melted down his silver: he had one ingot of fine-thread silver weighing twelve taels, and if anyone had loose silver handy, a swap would be ideal. His true aim was to swap with Sun. Sun asked to see it, and Wang readily produced a real silver ingot. Sun took it and said, "It really is golden-flower fine-thread." Wanting to prove the silver was genuine, Wang took it back from Sun and passed it around to everyone on the boat, asking, "Is it good?" They all agreed, "It's fine-thread." Since there happened to be a brush and inkstone on board, Wang gave a faint cold smile and wrote on the ingot: "Twelve taels, full weight, at the bottom of the wind-nest." Sun thought to himself, "What a flighty man—if you have silver, why fiddle with it like that?" So he quietly said to Wang, "A man out traveling should be more careful." Wang replied, "No harm done." Sun then asked, "What discount do you want on the swap?" Wang said, "I'm only buying sundry goods in small lots. Whatever fineness you judge it, brother, set the rate as you see fit." Sun took out small pieces weighing eight or nine qian each, about ninety-one or ninety-two percent pure. Wang looked at them and said happily, "Was this silver cast at ninety-four or ninety-five? If it's all like this, that will do nicely." Wang deliberately overestimated the fineness of Sun's silver to make him eager to swap. Sun fetched a balance, they weighed the two lots against each other, and the discount was settled clearly. Wang then took white cotton paper from his trunk and, together with Sun, wrapped the silver into two parcels. Pretending to get up, he turned away for a moment and deliberately "mistook" the parcels, slipping the original silver into his sleeve and saying, "This parcel is mine." Sun said, "No—this parcel is yours." Wang then switched in the fake, also wrapped in cotton paper and looking just like the real silver parcel, and handed it to Sun to keep. Sun took it, and though he slightly opened the tight wrapping and saw the writing on the silver looked the same, he did not examine it closely and locked it away in his trunk. Soon afterward, Wang went ashore and they parted. Sun traveled on to Nanjing, and when he took out the silver he had received, it was tin. He was sick with regret, but too late—only then did he realize the man had switched parcels and cheated him.

Note: Sun Tao was a simple, honest man. When he examined the silver, he only thought the other man flighty; he did not see that the flightiness was exactly the point. It kept people from suspecting anything, so the fake could be used later. Otherwise, once the swap was made, if someone nearby had picked up the silver for a look, wouldn't the scheme have collapsed? So the cold smile on the boat and the show of writing on the ingot were nothing but a trick to dazzle the eyes—after that, who would examine it closely again? Someone might ask: "Suppose that when the silver was being wrapped, Sun had taken the real silver into his own hand first and only then let Wang take his—wouldn't Wang have been stuck?" The answer: even so, a swindler like him has a hundred tricks; even with the real silver in Sun's hand, he would have found some other way to make off with it. Just keep to your own station, spend your own money, and never covet a small advantage—then you will not fall into the snare.

stories.title_en: A Daoist Swaps Out Gold on Board a Boat

paragraphs.en: Ben, a student of the Imperial Academy, was at the Southern Academy. With his term finished and about to head home, he wanted to exchange for several dozen taels of good gold to bring back as a gift to his wife and concubines in honor of his long journey. His fellow townsman Deng, also an Academy student, tried to stop him: 'People exchanging gold in the capital are forever being cheated by swindlers who pass off copper. You don't need the gold urgently—why exchange it here?' Ben said, "Only the capital has good gold. If any swindler can get the better of me, I'll grant he has real skill." Within a few days he had exchanged for more than ten taels of gold; each deal was checked against the gold's fineness, and all of it was good gold.

Later a young man came with a twelve-tael gold ingot to exchange. Ben took it and looked: it was nearly pure gold. He asked the rate, and the young man said, "A country gentleman ordered it exchanged; it must be done at a five-to-one rate." Ben passed it to Deng: "This gold could fetch six taels per tael; at five, the price is fair." Deng looked and said, "It really is good. Check this gold and put it away first—don't let it pass through his hands again—then weigh out sixty taels of silver to pay him." Ben followed the advice: he took in the gold first, then paid over the silver. The young man had no chance to work a switch and had to take the silver home. He told his father, "The two Academy students were so on their guard that I couldn't pull it off." The father stamped his foot: "Our whole family's living was in that ingot, and you've handed them our capital! How are we supposed to live? Quick—find out when this Academy student is heading home." The report came back: "They've already booked a boat; they board on a set day at a fixed hour." The information checked out.

On the appointed day, the two Imperial Academy students boarded the boat and settled in. The old con man had disguised himself as a Daoist priest, his robe and cap neat and clean, and came to take passage; the helmsman allowed him aboard. In conversation, the Daoist spoke with easy grace, and when talk turned to the affairs of officials and commoners in the capital, he knew it all inside out. The two Academy students and the other passengers enjoyed talking with him. Two days later, toward evening, the Daoist deliberately brought up methods for judging pearls, jade, and treasures, and everyone chatted idly for a while. Then the talk came around to judging gold, and he said he was an even better judge of that. Bi, the Academy student, boasted that in the capital he had exchanged for an ingot of pure gold, and at a bargain price besides. Some of the passengers asked to see it and estimate its fineness. Eager to show off, Bi took it out and passed it around, and everyone admired the fine gold. When all had looked their fill, the sky was growing dark and it was handed back to Bi. Just as he was about to put it into his trunk, the Daoist said, "May I have a look too?" He took it, glanced at it, and said, "It really is fine, true gold!" Then he handed it straight back and moved on to some fresh topic. Bi put the gold away. Dinner was ready, and they all scattered to eat. The next day the Daoist paid his fare to the helmsman, took leave of the company, and went ashore.

When Ben got home, he divided the gold as gifts among his wife and concubines. A few days later he called in a goldsmith to make bracelets and hair ornaments. First he had the small ingots worked, and the goldsmith praised the gold. Ben boasted, "I also exchanged for a twelve-tael ingot that is even better." The goldsmith said, "With big ingots in the capital, crooks often cheat people with copper." Ben said, "I'll fetch it for you to see—what swindler could cheat me?" The goldsmith took it in hand and laughed: "This is copper, all right." Ben was stunned; he snatched it back and looked: "It really is copper. Deng and I examined it and judged it first-rate gold, and everyone on the boat who saw it called it good gold—how were we all deceived?" Then it hit him: "Ah, that's it! The last one to look at it was that Daoist. When he handed it back, the sky was nearly dark; I never checked it again before locking it in the trunk. That is when it was switched! How did that Daoist come to have a piece of copper so alike, already in his hand, to make the switch so easily? The young swindler who exchanged the gold in the capital must have been the old crook's son. When the son couldn't pull off the switch at the exchange, the father came aboard to make the switch on the way home."

Note: As for the old con man making off with Ben's gold, people call this swindler a real master. I say otherwise. If Ben had kept it hidden and never shown it, then even with the divine cunning of a Zhuge Liang and the subtle wit of a Zhuangzi, how could the old crook have gotten the gold into his hands to look at it? How would he have made off with it? So the blame lies with Ben's own boasting and showing off—he invited the swindle himself. Ah.
